parts: Space organisation means assigning space to an activity and arranging systematically all the materials needed for it: allotting space, making all that is required available on the spot and arranging materials and equipment. It saves time and energy. Functional storage means storing the things for a task near where the task is done. Two activities done near each other can be dovetailed, for example washing utensils while food is cooking when water is in the kitchen, or cutting vegetables while watching TV. When space is limited, rooms are used for more than one purpose: a bedroom as a study during the day and a living room as a bedroom at night.

Household activities are cooking, washing clothes and utensils, sleeping, studying, playing and watching TV, and entertaining; each can be split into sub-activities (cooking: storing, pre-preparation, cooking, washing utensils, serving and storing left-overs). The area specified for an activity is a work centre; it does not need a separate room, and similar activities can share one room.

Cooking area: things used often are kept at a convenient height, heavy and frequently used containers (atta, rice) at floor level, and rarely used things in high places, called dead storage. Kitchen layouts: one-walled, two-walled (parallel), L-shaped and U-shaped; also sitting or standing kitchen. A folding dining table fixed on the wall saves space; the utensil washing area should be near the cooking area. Bathing area: storage for soaps, powders and toiletries, proper water supply and drainage, a sloping, non-slippery floor, electrical points away from water, space for a washing machine and soiled clothes and a clothesline near the washing area. Sleeping area: pull-out and trunk beds, bunk beds, folding beds, beds with drawers (preferably on wheels), side tables, a wall-fixed mirror instead of a dressing table, a built-in almirah up to the ceiling and a study table. Study area: good natural and artificial light, least disturbance, bookshelf along the wall. Entertainment area: drawing room divided into sitting and dining parts, a divider with shelves, sofa-cum-bed, diwan and folding beds. A one-room house must fit all work centres in one room, distinguishing the areas.

Guidelines for effective work centres: arrange in a sequential order (pre-preparation, washing, cooking, serving), use transparent or labelled storage containers, give adequate lighting and ventilation, make centres easy to clean, prefer built-in storage to cupboards, and create storage under the staircase, below window slabs and in lofts. Aesthetics: furniture to suit room size (small and light in a small room), an organised look, arrangement that does not hinder movement, furniture arranged by activity, good lighting (a well-lit small room looks spacious), distinguishing areas in a one-room flat, light colours and a white ceiling for dark small rooms, and decorative items and indoor plants.
